The reflection coefficient of the optimized multilayer absorbers is below -20 dB in many frequency subranges within 2-18 GHz.
Composite materials use epoxy resin with multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 weight percentages.
MWCNTs used are NANOCYL™ NC7000 with average diameter ~9.5 nm and length ~1.5 µm.
Dielectric properties were measured using a vector network analyzer with a coaxial air-line method.
Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) with mutation was used to optimize layer thickness and material selection.
Layer thickness ranges from 0 to 10 mm, with up to 10 layers allowed in the design.
Increasing MWCNT concentration increases both real and imaginary parts of permittivity, enhancing microwave absorption.
Ultrasonication at 20 kHz for 15 minutes was used to disperse MWCNTs in epoxy resin.
Polymerization of composite samples took about 16 hours at 50°C.
The optimized multilayer absorber acts as a cloak for cube satellites, simulated via finite element method in COMSOL.
The multilayer absorber reduces electromagnetic reflection and attenuates internal electric fields, improving interference immunity.
The PSO algorithm updates particle positions and velocities based on cognitive and social components with inertia weight decreasing from 0.9 to 0.4.
The mutation probability in PSO decreases linearly from 10% to 0.01% over iterations to avoid local minima.
Four cylindrical samples per material composition were measured to ensure repeatability of dielectric properties.
The loss factor (LF%) is defined as LF% = (1 - RC^2 - TC^2) * 100, where RC is reflection coefficient and TC is transmission coefficient.
Transmission coefficient (TC) is zero since the RAM is mounted on a metallic satellite surface.
The study balances electromagnetic absorption capability with practical manufacturing considerations and cost.
The PSO optimization considers both normal and oblique incidence angles for TM and TE modes.
The database of composite materials includes measured dielectric properties used as input for PSO.
The research integrates nanomaterials, electromagnetic theory, composite manufacturing, and computational optimization.
